candidate.title: Pursuit
candidate.problemStatement: Long-running real-world agent work is repeatedly represented by provider sessions, goals, task cards, issues, traces, and mutable prose, none of which reliably preserve one intended-change identity across revisions, actors, actions, evidence, pause, and recovery.
candidate.scope: A provisional generic continuity object behind profiles such as Atlas Go. The name, universal minimum closure, cross-domain applicability, novelty, and Primitive status remain open.

observationPerspective.bearer: agent or operator viewing work through one task card, chat, session, or provider goal
observationPerspective.proximity: inside one execution surface but outside the full cross-session continuity
consequences: bears context loss, scope reconstruction, handoff, recovery, and completion ambiguity

genesis.observation: Separating context, authorization, and execution history from a long-running Atlas Go still left one necessary object: the stable identity of an intended reality change whose current specification can be revised while the work remains recognizable across agents and execution providers.
genesis.candidateObject: A Pursuit is the durable identity of an intended reality change across revisions, actors, actions, and evidence.
genesis.claimBoundary: This cut records a provisional continuity-object hypothesis grounded in maintainer experience and structural analysis. It does not establish a universal work ontology, final name, historical novelty, product readiness, or accepted Primitive status.

transformedPerspective.bearer: human and agents jointly continuing one intended change across sessions and providers
transformedPerspective.proximity: inside the continuity, revision, and recovery burden
consequences: bears identity drift, intent revision, attribution, resumption, and settlement consequences

genesis.transformation: The observer moved from one provider's current task representation to the participant responsible for preserving one intended change across many representations and executions.
genesis.newlyVisibleNeed: A stable work identity must survive provider goals and mutable projections while material intent changes produce exact successor roots rather than retroactively changing old context or authority.
genesis.methodNotes: The original fused Proof-Carrying Work Object was decomposed after Warrant, Atlas, and Episode responsibilities were removed and an intended-change continuity object still remained.

contactSides: one execution session, agent, provider goal, or task projection
future agents, operators, tools, and settlement processes continuing the same intended change
boundaryPressure.implicitHandling: Continuity is reconstructed from mutable task prose, chat history, issue state, branch names, human memory, and provider-specific identifiers.

pressureChanges.description: Different humans and agents increasingly continue the same work without sharing transient context.
Long-running and multi-agent work creates many provider-local goals, sessions, and task projections for one intended change.
The same work crosses repositories, devices, models, task systems, and domain vocabularies.
Identity or scope drift changes what work is attributed, authorized, assessed, and declared complete.

observedFailures: A new agent cannot tell whether two task records continue the same intended change.
Editing mutable scope text silently changes the meaning of prior approval and evidence.
A provider goal disappears while the real work remains active.
Execution completion is mistaken for satisfaction of the enduring intent.
boundaryPressure.mediationClaim: A stable Pursuit reference plus immutable successor intent roots may preserve intended-change continuity while allowing provider-specific task and goal projections.
boundaryPressure.internalObjectAlternative: The same behavior may be implemented by disciplined issue, case, workflow, or event-sourced aggregate contracts without a distinct Pursuit Primitive.

pressure: Mutable task descriptions expanding prior meaning
Provider-local goals failing to survive the real work lifecycle
Need to join context, authorization, episodes, and settlement to one stable intended change
grounding.evidenceBoundary: Public reconstruction of maintainer experience with long-running agent work and the ontology split recorded on 2026-07-17. No independent adopter, cross-domain implementation, benchmark, or universal deletion test is included.
knownGaps: No final name or proven universal minimum closure
No measured comparison with issue, case, workflow, or provider-goal alternatives
No proof that acceptance and safety belong in every Pursuit profile
No common runtime contract for intent-root revision and relation semantics

alternatives.name: Work or work item
alternatives.reason: This is the safest generic vocabulary but may conflate intended continuity, performed activity, and produced result.

alternatives.name: Goal, task, issue, case, incident, job, or plan
alternatives.reason: These may be sufficient domain profiles, or their repeated cross-domain structure may indicate a shared underlying object.

alternatives.name: Purpose or intent
alternatives.reason: Purpose explains why and intent specifies one cut, but neither clearly preserves the identity that survives intent revision.

alternatives.name: Event-sourced workflow aggregate
alternatives.reason: A generic aggregate with domain events may implement the required behavior without a separately named Primitive.

alternatives.name: No new Primitive
alternatives.reason: The continuity may be a common product requirement rather than an independently useful object.

contractModel.identity: A stable pursuit_ref for one intended reality change, with immutable intent_root successors for material revisions.
contractModel.boundary: Purpose, desired change, current intent root, scope, acceptance or settlement conditions, safety boundaries, and typed parent, dependency, and successor relations; context, authorization, execution history, and provider projections remain external references.
contractModel.authority: Creating or revising a Pursuit declares an intended change but does not itself authorize execution, certify facts, or decide completion. Those responsibilities remain with Warrant, evidence, assessment, and authorized decision processes.
contractModel.lifecycle: proposed -> available or active -> paused or revised -> settled, abandoned, or superseded; exact state vocabulary remains profile-dependent

minimumClosure.notes: Stable identity and successor intent roots appear load-bearing, but purpose, acceptance, safety, and relation fields have not survived non-isomorphic domain implementations.

deletion.notes: Without a continuity object, Atlas selection, Warrant subject binding, Episode attribution, and settlement each need another task identity, but existing issue or case systems may already supply it.

fuse.notes: Task, case, incident, investigation, and Go appear related, but no shared contract has been implemented across them.

falsifiers: Provider goals or ordinary issue systems preserve all required continuity without repeated reconstruction.
Intent-root versioning creates more coordination cost than scope drift prevents.
Non-software domains require incompatible identity or lifecycle semantics.
Pursuit cannot be separated cleanly from Mission, workflow, or actor commitment.
The object has no reusable operations beyond generic event-sourced aggregate behavior.
Users or agents cannot map their work without unnatural mandatory fields.

dogfood.notes: Long-running Atlas Go experience motivates the candidate, but this public cut contains no common Pursuit runtime contract or comparative qualification.

decision.reason: Removing Atlas, Warrant, Episode, and provider-goal responsibilities leaves a coherent intended-change continuity object, but naming, minimum closure, transfer, deletion, fuse, and dogfood evidence remain unresolved.
residualRisks: The candidate may rename an ordinary work-item aggregate.
Atlas Go experience may overfit software and maintainer workflow.
The poetic name may obscure simpler domain vocabulary.
A universal schema may force bounded-task assumptions onto exploration or continuing processes.
Identity revision rules may become administrative burden rather than useful compression.
